source.title: The Price of Robustness: Stable Classifiers Need Overparameterization
source.authors: Jonas von Berg; Adalbert Fono; Massimiliano Datres; Sohir Maskey; G. Kutyniok

page_placements.theme: Optimization settings and measurement choices affect observed trajectories

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double descent as background and studies stability as network width changes, but it does not test any listed double-descent version: it reports no model-size, epoch, or sample-size test-error curve around an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The paper’s own experiments report width-dependent stability and normalized co-stability, and describe their qualitative relation to test accuracy. These measures and results do not establish the fall-rise-fall test-error behavior in the listed versions. The double-descent statements in the introduction are background, not new results.
record.test_reason: Double descent appears only as motivation in the introduction and in a cited remark (Remark 14). The experiments measure class stability and normalized co-stability across widths. All models are trained to at least 99% training accuracy, so every width sits past the interpolation threshold. No test-error curve over size, epochs or samples is reported, and no peak region is probed. Stability is a related construct, not test error.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The paper's main contribution is theoretical. It proves stability-based generalization bounds and a law of robustness for discontinuous classifiers: interpolating with p≈n parameters forces instability, and high stability requires p of order nd. Experiments show stability and normalized co-stability rising with width and tracking test accuracy, while norm-based measures do not.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments measure stability and co-stability across network widths; they do not reproduce the original double-descent interventions or test-error measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported stability scaling varies with dataset, architecture, activation, depth, training duration, and Gaussian-data variance. On 8-layer MNIST MLPs, varying training duration produced an initial decrease at small widths; fixed seven-epoch training restored the stated scaling. Larger Gaussian variance weakened or disrupted the width trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Class stability and normalized co-stability increase with width in interpolating MLPs and CNNs on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The authors say these measures qualitatively track test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the overparameterized interpolating regime, input-space margin (class stability) grows with width and tracks test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: On 8-layer MNIST MLPs, an initial stability drop at small widths is attributed to unequal training durations. It disappears with fixed seven-epoch training or with widths up to 16384.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width-stability trends are confounded by training duration when models are trained only to a fixed training-accuracy target.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gaussian toy data with large variance (large isoperimetric scale), stability becomes non-monotonic in width and falls at large widths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of width for class stability depends on the data's isoperimetric scale.

record.problems: The stability values are based on adversarial-attack estimates; when attacks fail within the maximum radius, the assigned value induces a downward bias, so the authors describe the estimates as conservative lower bounds. Most plotted values are not numerically stated in the text. Test accuracy is described as around 50% for CIFAR-10, without per-width values. The authors note that confirming the Gaussian variance behavior would require broader width ranges and more complex datasets.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over model size; all widths are already near-interpolating, and test accuracy is given only as 'around 50%' with a qualitative trend (R17).
No test error over training epochs.
No risk-versus-capacity curve across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
No label-noise or regularization manipulation of a test-error peak. The Gaussian-variance experiment concerns stability, not test error.
No re-counting of parameters or effective-parameter curve.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. R17 (test accuracy vs width) is qualitative only and covers only post-interpolation widths, so it cannot show a peak. Remark 14 cites others' reports that Lipschitz constants show double descent (Gamba et al.). That is a cited result, not this study's own. 'cites_only' would also be defensible, but the introduction does explain double descent, so 'discusses' is kept.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error curve over model size or evidence about a peak near interpolation.
No test-error curve over training epochs.
No test-error comparison across training-sample sizes near interpolation.
No risk-versus-capacity curve testing double descent across model classes.
No test of whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
No test of noise or regularization effects on double-descent peaks, or of triple/multiple descent.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters or test of the resulting curve shape.

relation.reason: Double descent motivates the introduction and appears in Remark 14 as a finding from cited work; the study does not test or operationally use it.

tranche.reason: The study tests stability-based robustness laws and width-dependent stability scaling, without testing any double-descent claim version.

source_check.notes: The reported training criterion is at least 99% accuracy, described as near-interpolation; it does not establish that every width lies past an exact interpolation threshold. Stability estimates are attack-based conservative lower bounds.

statements.correction: 8-layer MNIST MLPs; initial stability decrease at small widths; unequal training durations of up to seven epochs for narrow models and two for the widest models; extended sweep to width 16384 recovers monotonic scaling at sufficiently large widths with similar epoch counts; fixed seven-epoch training restores scaling across the full width range; same effects for normalized co-stability.
statements.problem: The extended-width experiment recovers monotonic scaling at sufficiently large widths; the text does not say it removes the small-width drop. Fixed seven-epoch training restores scaling across the full width range.
